If you have a strong stomach for schmaltz, or you’re able to focus your attention on individual trees in its sugarplum forest, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button does indeed contain moments of beauty and delight.
Unfortunately, there is a lot of strangely inert musical theater between those two moments.
It’s one of the most alive musicals you’re likely to see this season with words and melodies that feel drawn from the wisdom and heartbeat of the ages.
Of the three new musicals noted above, I’d put my money on this one having a great white way in its future.
It's been some time since a musical has made such a bold claim on our emotions.
The Curious Case of Benjamin Button can eagerly await a tidal wave of long-run audiences.
They convincingly buy into the fanciful premise, taking us on a fast-paced, thoughtful journey examining the mysteries of aging and time itself.
This is Benjamin Button as we’ve never seen him before.
The Curious Case of Benjamin Button is a charmer of a musical that possesses distinct Come from Away vibes.
It is the universally strong performances by the ensemble, and the show's heartfelt message of making the most of whatever life hands you, that carry the day.
It wouldn’t be a waste to spend part of it at this musical.

The British musical by Jethro Compton and Darren Clark, which had an award-winning run on the West End, has the feel of an epic English folk tale, set in a remote fishing village in rural Cornwall, England.
These “criticisms” are more frustrations than complaints, since there is plenty to both like and admire about “Benjamin Button.”
This new musical is a powerful reinterpretation of the tale, weaving a complex narrative with an infectious score...
The show is whimsical, uproarious, and, above all, genuinely fun.

Plus, the production brims with an old-fashioned craftsmanship, from Compton's wood- and fishnet-lined sets to Anna Kelsey's costumes to Zoe Spurr's lighting (which mesmerizes in sequences set at sea and underwater).
Fortunately, writer/director Jethro Compton is as skilled at focusing on the small and intimate moments of a man’s life as he is at staging a town’s worth of hubbub.
Andrew Durand, Kelsee Kimmel, and an ensemble of actor-musicians make a warm case for this Olivier winner, even as its clock-watching book crowds the romance at its center.

With its stunning music, extraordinary ensemble, and inventive visual storytelling, it’s a rare musical that leaves you thinking not only about the lives unfolding onstage but about the people and moments that give your own life meaning.
For that reason alone, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button deserves to be seen not just as a fleeting curiosity.
For the best experience of this musical, just sink into your seat and let the tides take you.

cn.t: This Olivier-winning British import charms critics with its Celtic folk score and heartfelt storytelling, though some find the musical's relentless folksy tone repetitive and its earnestness at odds with Fitzgerald's satirical source material.
